index.hero_subtitle: Clear, honest information for immigrants, refugees, and international protection applicants living in Ireland. Healthcare, housing, legal aid, employment — your rights, explained.
index.story_quote: A gentleman came in for a fan. That wasn't the reason. That's why I started this.
index.story_context: This website began in a GP clinic in Ennis, County Clare, when a patient — an international protection applicant — was told he needed a doctor's letter just to have a fan in his room. Something as basic as sleeping comfortably had become a bureaucratic battle. That moment revealed a wider truth: too many people in Ireland's protection system don't know their rights, don't know where to turn, and are asked to jump through humiliating hoops for basic dignity. Sahl Health Ed exists to change that.
index.quick_access_title: What Do You Need Help With?
index.card_rights_desc: What the law says about your accommodation, the standards you are entitled to, and when a doctor's letter is — and isn't — required.
index.card_health_desc: How to register with a GP, get a medical card, access mental health services, and understand your healthcare rights.
index.card_emergency_desc: Suicide helplines, domestic violence support, victim services, and organisations that will stand with you.
index.card_legal_desc: Free legal help, how to complain about your accommodation, and who to contact when something feels wrong.
index.num_emergency_note: Gardaí, Ambulance, Fire, Coast Guard. Free call.
index.num_legal_note: Free legal aid for asylum seekers. Mon–Fri.
index.dignity_lead: Under Irish and EU law, international protection applicants have the right to adequate accommodation, healthcare, and a dignified standard of living. No one can lawfully deny you basic amenities because you are an immigrant.
index.fan_box_title: Did a hostel or centre ask you for a doctor's letter for something basic?
index.fan_box_text: There is no legal requirement in the Reception Conditions Regulations for a GP letter to approve basic items like a fan, a room change for comfort, or standard living equipment. The only formal medical letter protocol applies to transfer requests between centres — and even then, it requires a consultant's letter, not a GP note.

rights.page_subtitle: Clear, factual information about what you are legally entitled to as an international protection applicant — and what nobody has the right to demand from you.
rights.law_lead: Ireland's obligations to people seeking international protection come from the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230/2018). This law implements the EU Reception Conditions Directive and sets minimum standards for accommodation, healthcare, food, and living conditions.
rights.law_key_text: Regulation 4(1): You are entitled to material reception conditions (accommodation, meals, money) "whereby they do not have sufficient means to attain an adequate standard of living." The State must ensure your accommodation guarantees "a dignified standard of living" and "adequate living space."
rights.medical_title: Medical Letters: What Is — and Isn't — Required
rights.medical_warning_text: There is NO legal or regulatory requirement for a GP letter to approve basic amenities like an electric fan, a comfortable room temperature, or standard living equipment. If a hostel or centre demands a doctor's letter for something basic, they are enforcing an internal policy, not a law.
rights.protocol_title: The ONLY Official Medical Letter Protocol
rights.protocol_intro: IPAS has one formal protocol involving medical letters: the Protocol for Medical Transfer Requests, introduced in January 2024. This applies only to:
protocol_list: Requests to move from one accommodation centre to another
Where the move is essential for health reasons
Requires a letter from a hospital consultant (not a GP)
The letter must state the move is essential, not just preferable
IPAS then reviews this with an Independent Medical Referee
rights.protocol_note: Even for transfers, many requests are refused unless there is a significant medical vulnerability or safety concern.
rights.table_fan: Requesting a fan for your room
rights.table_fan_law: Basic living amenity. No statutory requirement.
rights.table_room: Requesting a room change within centre
rights.table_room_law: Centre manager discretion; not a medical matter.
rights.table_transfer: Requesting transfer to another centre for health
rights.table_work_law: IPAS policy: transfers only for "exceptional circumstances"
rights.table_healthcare_law: You have a legal right to healthcare under Reg. 18.
rights.accommodation_intro: Since January 2024, HIQA (Health Information and Quality Authority) independently inspects permanent IPAS centres against the legally binding National Standards for Accommodation. These standards cover:
rights.acc_space_desc: Adequate room size, privacy, ventilation, and temperature control. Rooms should be safe and habitable.
rights.acc_food_desc: Nutritious meals or self-catering facilities. Access to clean drinking water and food storage.
rights.acc_safety_desc: Fire safety, protection from abuse, and procedures to keep vulnerable people safe.
rights.acc_needs_desc: Assessment and response to disabilities, mental health needs, pregnancy, and family circumstances.
rights.ombudsman_quote: The Office of the Ombudsman has recommended that protection applicants should have own-door accommodation with adequate living space and access to their own cooking facilities. While this ideal is not yet fully realised, it is the official benchmark against which complaints are judged.
rights.emergency_warning_text: As of early 2026, IPAS operates 312 properties across Ireland, but only approximately 49 are permanent centres. The remainder are emergency or pre-reception facilities. HIQA only inspects permanent centres. If you are in emergency accommodation, your remedy is through the complaints process and the Ombudsman — not HIQA inspection. This distinction is critical.
rights.complain_intro: You have a legal right to make a complaint without fear of retaliation. The process is:
rights.complain_1_text: Try to resolve the issue informally first. If that fails, make a formal written complaint. They must respond within 14 days.
rights.complain_2_text: Email ipasinbox@justice.ie with your name, TRC number, and full details of your complaint.
rights.complain_3_text: If IPAS does not resolve your complaint, you can go to the Office of the Ombudsman online, by post, or by phone at 01 636 5600. You must do this within 12 months.
rights.complain_4_text: If your complaint relates to a child, contact the Ombudsman for Children's Office instead.
rights.retaliation_text: Your entitlement to accommodation cannot be reduced or withdrawn simply because you made a complaint. If this happens, contact the Ombudsman immediately and document everything.
rights.super_ipas_role: Runs the accommodation system; contracts private operators
rights.super_dcedy_contact: Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth
rights.super_hiqa_role: Independent inspector of permanent centres since Jan 2024
rights.allowances_intro: As an international protection applicant in Direct Provision, you are entitled to:
rights.allow_adult: Daily Expenses Allowance: €38.80 per week for adults
rights.allow_child_benefit: Child Benefit: If you have children, you may also be entitled to Irish Child Benefit
rights.allow_note: Note: If you take up paid employment, your Daily Expenses Allowance may be reduced proportionally. As of late 2025, the government proposed requiring contributions toward accommodation costs from those earning above certain thresholds. Check gov.ie for current rules.
rights.interpreter_text: You have a legal right to interpretation in your asylum interviews with the International Protection Office (IPO), in medical settings, and in legal proceedings. If you are not offered an interpreter, ask for one. Do not let anyone pressure you to proceed without adequate interpretation.
rights.travel_text: Protection applicants generally cannot leave Ireland without permission while their application is being processed. If you leave without permission, your application may be deemed withdrawn. If you need to travel for an emergency (e.g., family death, serious illness), contact the International Protection Office before making any travel arrangements.
rights.tip_text: If you are being asked for unreasonable documentation (like a GP letter for a fan), ask the staff member to show you the written policy or regulation that requires it. If they cannot, that tells you it is not a legal requirement. Keep copies of all letters, emails, and notes of conversations.

services.page_subtitle: You don't have to face this alone. These organisations provide free, confidential support — regardless of your immigration status.
services.svc_emergency_desc: Gardaí, Ambulance, Fire, Coast Guard. Free from any phone.
services.svc_samaritans_desc: 24/7 confidential listening. Whatever you're going through, you can talk. Free call.
services.svc_pieta_desc: Suicide and self-harm crisis helpline. 24/7. Free. Professional counsellors.
services.svc_text_desc: Free 24/7 text service for anyone in crisis. Anonymous.
services.svc_hse_mh_desc: National 24/7 mental health helpline. Your GP can also refer you to local mental health services.
services.svc_spirasi_desc: Specialist support for survivors of torture and trauma. Medico-legal reports, therapy, rehabilitation. Dublin-based.
services.svc_jrs_desc: Psychosocial support, outreach to Direct Provision centres, language support, and integration programmes.
services.svc_turning_desc: Counselling and therapy for people from refugee and asylum-seeking backgrounds. Culturally sensitive support.
services.svc_doras_desc: Free, confidential support for migrants who have experienced crime — hate crime, domestic violence, trafficking, labour exploitation. Interpreter support available.
services.svc_womensaid_desc: 24/7 helpline for women experiencing domestic abuse. Free and confidential.
services.svc_rape_desc: 24/7 support for survivors of sexual violence. Free and confidential.
services.svc_trafficking_desc: Blue Blindfold campaign. Free, confidential, available in multiple languages.
services.svc_safe_desc: National network of domestic violence services. Find your local service.
services.svc_lgbt_desc: Support and information for LGBTQ+ people in Ireland. Confidential helpline.
services.svc_ncp_desc: Employment rights support, citizenship applications, social welfare help, education and accommodation support. National network.
services.svc_mrci_desc: Employment rights, anti-exploitation, advocacy for undocumented workers, and integration support.
services.svc_intreo_desc: After 6 months in the protection process, you may apply for Labour Market Access Permission. Visit your local Intreo centre or gov.ie for forms. Minimum wage: €13.50/hour (as of Jan 2025).
services.svc_cisc_desc: Local Ennis-based support. Outreach to Clare Lodge and other centres. Advocacy, translation, accompanied visits.
services.svc_etb_desc: Free English language (ESOL) classes and adult education nationwide. Contact your local ETB.
services.svc_nasc_desc: Integration support, rights information, and advocacy for migrants in Ireland.
services.svc_irc_desc: Information, advocacy, and integration support. Information hub for protection applicants.
services.svc_crosscare_desc: Major national support NGO. Information, advocacy, and practical support for migrants.
services.local_cisc_addr: Unit 6, Clonroad Business Park, Ennis, Co. Clare
services.local_cisc_langs: Services available in Arabic, French, and English. Dedicated outreach to Clare Lodge and King Thomond DP Centre.
services.local_ico_desc: Processes asylum applications. Not an advocacy body — this is the decision-maker.
services.local_ipat_desc: If your application is refused, you appeal to IPAT within 15 working days.

health.page_subtitle: Everyone in Ireland's international protection system has the right to healthcare — including free GP visits, hospital care, and prescription medicines.
health.rights_lead: Under Regulation 18 of the Reception Conditions Regulations 2018, you have the right to:
rights_list: Mental health care assessed as necessary
Other healthcare to maintain your health
health.prescription_text: If you live in Direct Provision and have a medical card, you do not pay prescription charges. Normally medical card holders pay a small charge per item, but this is waived for IPAS residents.
health.access_1_text: Apply through the HSE. If you live in Direct Provision, you are entitled to a medical card. Ask your centre manager or GP for help with the application. You can also apply online at hse.ie.
health.access_2_text: Most IPAS centres have a GP who visits regularly, or residents are assigned to a local GP practice. If GP lists are full, the HSE will arrange access to a GP with availability in your area. This is free with your medical card.
health.access_3_text: You are entitled to free care in public hospitals. If you need to go to hospital, your GP will refer you. In an emergency, go to A&E or call 112/999.
health.access_4_text: Medical card holders get limited free dental and optical services: basic extractions, one eye test every 2 years, and limited glasses/contacts subsidy. Major dental work (crowns, bridges) is generally not covered. Ask your GP or local health centre for a referral.
health.interpreter_text: You have the right to an interpreter for GP and hospital appointments. Ask when booking. Do not let anyone tell you to 'bring a friend' instead. Professional interpretation is your right and ensures accuracy.
health.mh_lead: Living in the protection system can be stressful, lonely, and frightening. Asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness. You have the right to mental health support, and it will not affect your asylum application.
health.mh_gp_desc: Your GP can refer you to counselling, psychiatry, or psychology services. This is free with your medical card.
health.mh_hse_desc: Free national mental health helpline. Available 24/7. You can also text 50808.
health.mh_spirasi_desc: For survivors of torture and severe trauma. Therapy, rehabilitation, and medico-legal support.
health.mh_dp_desc: Some centres have on-site counselling. Ask your centre manager or welfare officer what mental health services are available.
health.confidential_text: What you tell your doctor is private. Your GP cannot share your medical information with IPAS, the International Protection Office, or the Department of Justice without your consent — except in very rare situations where there is a serious risk to life. Seeking mental health support will not negatively affect your asylum claim.
health.screening_lead: When you first arrive in Ireland, you are offered voluntary health screening at the reception centre. This checks for:
health.screening_note: This screening is voluntary and confidential. The results do not affect your asylum application.
health.daily_title: Taking Care of Your Health Day-to-Day
health.daily_sleep_desc: Good sleep is essential. If noise, temperature, or room conditions are affecting your sleep, document it and raise it with your centre manager. Poor sleep affects mental and physical health.
health.daily_food_desc: If you have dietary needs (religious, medical, allergies), tell your centre manager. Centres are required to cater for dietary requirements.
health.daily_move_desc: Physical activity reduces stress. Walking, stretching, or any exercise you enjoy helps. Many centres have outdoor space — use it if you can.
health.daily_connect_desc: Isolation harms health. Connect with others in your centre, local community groups, or support organisations. Clare Immigrant Support Centre runs outreach to Clare Lodge.
health.srh_lead: You have the right to access sexual health services, maternity care, and family planning. These services are confidential and free with your medical card.
health.srh_maternity: Maternity care: Fully free for medical card holders. Tell your centre manager early if you are pregnant so they can plan appropriate accommodation.
health.srh_contraception: Contraception: Free for women aged 17–35. Discuss with your GP.
health.srh_sti: STI testing: Free and confidential at public sexual health clinics. Find your nearest clinic at hse.ie/sexual-health.
health.children_text: Children in IPAS are entitled to the same health services as all children in Ireland: public health nurse visits, developmental checks, school health screenings, vaccinations, and specialist referrals. Ensure your children are registered with a GP.
health.addiction_text: If you or someone you know is struggling with alcohol or drugs, HSE addiction services are free and confidential. Your GP can refer you, or contact the HSE Drugs & Alcohol Helpline: 1800 459 459.

legal.page_subtitle: You have the right to legal help. Whether it's your asylum case, a complaint about your accommodation, or a problem at work, there are people who will help you for free.
legal.free_title: Free Legal Help for Asylum Seekers
legal.free_lead: If you are in the international protection process, you are entitled to free legal aid through the Legal Aid Board and its Refugee Legal Service (RLS).
legal.rls_desc: Free legal representation for international protection applicants. They can help with your asylum application, appeals, and judicial reviews.
legal.lab_desc: General civil legal aid — family law, housing, employment, and more. Free if you cannot afford a private solicitor.
legal.flac_desc: Free Legal Advice Centres. Drop-in clinics across Ireland for basic legal advice. Independent and confidential.
legal.irc_legal_desc: Information, advocacy, and casework support. Not a law firm, but they know the system and can guide you.
legal.ipo_desc: The IPO processes your asylum application. They are not your advocate — they are the decision-maker. You must cooperate with them, attend interviews, and respond to requests. If you move, tell them your new address immediately.
legal.ipat_desc: If the IPO refuses your application, you can appeal to IPAT. You have 15 working days from the date of the refusal letter to submit your appeal. Do not miss this deadline. Contact the Refugee Legal Service immediately if you receive a refusal.
legal.trc_desc: Your TRC is the plastic card you received when you claimed asylum. It is your ID in Ireland. Keep it safe. You need it to: register with a GP, collect your PPS number, access services, and prove your status. If you lose it, contact IPAS immediately.
legal.complain_title: How to Complain About Your Accommodation
legal.complain_intro: If you believe your centre is not meeting standards, treating you unfairly, or asking for unreasonable things (like a doctor's letter for a basic fan), you have a legal right to complain. Here is the proper process:
legal.comp_1_text: Speak to the manager first. Many issues can be resolved quickly. Keep a note of what was said and when.
legal.comp_2_text: If informal discussion fails, submit a written complaint. The manager must respond within 14 days. Use the centre's complaint form if they have one. Keep a copy.
legal.comp_3_text: Email ipasinbox@justice.ie with: your full name and TRC number; the name of your centre; a clear description of the problem; copies of any previous correspondence.
legal.comp_4_text:
If IPAS does not resolve your complaint, escalate to the Ombudsman. You must do this within 12 months.

Online: ombudsman.ie
Phone: 01 636 5600
Post: Office of the Ombudsman, 6 Earlsfort Terrace, Dublin 2, D02 W773
legal.comp_5_text: If your complaint involves a child, contact the OCO at oco.ie or 01 865 6800.
legal.comp_docs_title: 📝 What to Include in Your Complaint
comp_docs_list: Your name, TRC number, and contact details
The name and address of your accommodation centre
What happened, when, and who was involved
What you want to happen now
Copies of any letters, emails, or photos that support your case
solicitor_list: Your international protection application has been refused
You want to appeal to the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT)
You are facing deportation or removal
You want to apply for judicial review
You have been a victim of crime and need legal support
You have an employment or housing dispute
legal.deadline_warning_text: Legal deadlines in the asylum system are strict. If you receive a refusal letter, you usually have 15 working days to appeal. Do not wait. Contact the Refugee Legal Service or a solicitor immediately.
legal.bogus_text: Be careful of people who claim they can 'fast-track' your asylum claim or guarantee a positive result for money. Only registered solicitors and the Refugee Legal Service can legally represent you. If someone asks for cash to 'fix' your case, they are likely fraudulent. Report suspicious activity to the Gardaí or MRCI.
legal.advocacy_title: Organisations That Can Advocate For You
legal.adv_nasc_role: Migrant rights, legal information, anti-racism work
legal.adv_ihrec_role: Human rights and equality oversight — can take strategic cases
legal.work_lead: If you have Labour Market Access Permission, you have the same employment rights as any other worker in Ireland:
work_list: Minimum wage (€13.50 per hour as of Jan 2025 — check gov.ie for current rate)
Protection from unfair dismissal (after qualifying period)
Right to join a trade union
legal.work_exploit: If your employer is exploiting you — not paying you properly, making you work unsafe hours, or threatening you because of your immigration status — contact MRCI (01 889 7570) or the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) (059 917 8990) before confronting your employer. If you are undocumented, seek advice first.
legal.work_tip_text: If your employer threatens to report your immigration status because you asserted your employment rights, this may be penalisation and you can report it to MRCI or the WRC. However, if you are undocumented, seek advice before making a complaint to understand your risks.

about.page_subtitle: This website was born from one moment in a GP clinic — and the realisation that information is power, and too many people don't have either.
about.story_quote: A gentleman came in for a fan. That wasn't the reason.
about.story_p1: He was an international protection applicant living in Clare Lodge, Ennis. He worked at night. He needed to sleep during the day. The room was hot. He asked for a fan — a €20 piece of plastic that would let him rest.
about.story_p2: The hostel said no. Unless a doctor wrote a letter saying he "needed" it.
about.story_p3: Another doctor had written that letter a few weeks before. Now they wanted a renewal. As if the room had suddenly become cool. As if his need for sleep had an expiry date.
about.story_p4: The patient wasn't the problem. The system was.
about.story_p5: That moment made it clear: there are people in Ireland's protection system who are asked to jump through humiliating hoops for basic dignity. Who don't know that a GP letter for a fan is not a legal requirement. Who don't know where to turn when someone says no.
about.story_p6: Sahl Health Ed exists to close that gap.
about.privacy_text: The story that inspired this site is real, but details have been changed to protect the individual's identity. No names, dates, or identifying characteristics are published. This is not about one person. It is about a pattern — and a system that makes ordinary needs feel like extraordinary demands.
about.believe_info_desc: Knowing your rights is the first step to defending them. We believe clear, honest information can be as powerful as any lawyer or politician.
about.believe_dignity_desc: A fan is not a luxury. A decent night's sleep is not a privilege. Suitable accommodation is not a favour. These are rights, and we will say so loudly.
about.believe_ireland_desc: Ireland has legal obligations under EU law to provide adequate, dignified reception conditions. When the gap between law and reality is this wide, something is broken — and silence is complicity.
about.believe_gp_desc: GPs, nurses, and carers see the human cost of bureaucratic cruelty. We believe healthcare professionals have a unique duty — and a unique power — to advocate for patients beyond the clinic door.
about.whatis_1_not: A law firm or solicitor's office
about.whatis_2_is: Based on publicly available legal and policy sources
about.whatis_3_is: Focused on immigrant rights and protections
about.whatis_3_not: A substitute for professional legal or medical advice
about.whatis_4_not: Funded by or affiliated with any government body
about.sources_intro: All information on this site is drawn from publicly available sources, including:
sources_list: HIQA inspection reports and National Standards for Accommodation
Office of the Ombudsman — Direct Provision updates and commentary
Irish Refugee Council reports and policy briefings
about.sources_correction: If you spot an error, an outdated fact, or something we've missed, please let us know. Accurate information saves time, stress, and dignity.
about.involve_intro: This site is a starting point, not a finish line. If you are:
involve_list: A healthcare worker who sees similar issues and wants to share resources
A translator who can help make this information available in more languages
A legal professional who can review or contribute
A community organiser with local knowledge to share
Someone who just wants to help
about.involve_cta: Get in touch. This is a collective effort.
